subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Why Is There Something Rather Than Nothing?
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why Is There Something Rather Than Nothing? usable.

hook.text: The Big Bang should have created equal parts matter and antimatter—which would annihilate, leaving nothing.

buildup.text: But a tiny imbalance meant for every billion antimatter particles, there were a billion and one matter particles.

discovery.text: That one-in-a-billion surplus is everything—every galaxy, star, planet, and person. The rest annihilated.

twist.text: We don't know what caused the asymmetry. It's one of the deepest unsolved problems in physics.

climax.text: Experiments at CERN search for differences between matter and antimatter behavior that could explain the imbalance.

punchline.text: One extra particle per billion. That tiny surplus is everything.

quiz.question: Why does matter exist at all after the Big Bang?
options: A tiny asymmetry produced slightly more matter than antimatter
The Big Bang only created matter, not antimatter
Dark energy prevented antimatter from forming

details.summary: The question of why anything exists at all is both physics' deepest mystery and an ancient philosophical puzzle. In physics terms, the Big Bang should have produced equal amounts of matter and antimatter that would annihilate completely — yet matter slightly dominated, and the observable universe…
details.whyItMatters: This matter-antimatter asymmetry (baryogenesis) is an unsolved problem in physics. Explaining why matter won over antimatter is essential to understanding why stars, planets, and life exist at all.
takeaways: Equal matter and antimatter should have annihilated completely
A tiny asymmetry allowed matter to survive and form the universe
Explaining this asymmetry is one of physics' biggest unsolved problems

faq.question: How big was the matter-antimatter asymmetry?
faq.answer: Incredibly tiny — for every billion antimatter particles, there were a billion and one matter particles. That extra one-in-a-billion surplus survived after annihilation and constitutes all the matter in the observable universe today: every galaxy, star, planet, and atom.

faq.question: What might have caused the asymmetry?
faq.answer: Andrei Sakharov identified three necessary conditions: baryon number violation, CP symmetry violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium. Known CP violation in particle physics is too small to explain the asymmetry. New physics — perhaps from undiscovered particles or interactions — is needed.
